AI Video Generation Prompt:

A cinematic luxury modest fashion commercial featuring a beautiful young woman wearing a beige hijab, elegant cream oversized blouse, and flowing blue denim maxi skirt. She walks confidently through a modern city street surrounded by contemporary architecture and stylish urban buildings.

Create a sequence of professional fashion-film shots:

* Full-body front shot of the woman walking naturally toward the camera.

* Close-up details of her elegant blouse, wristwatch, and accessories.

* Slow-motion close-up of her skirt moving naturally as she walks.

* Wide cinematic shot of her crossing a busy city street.

* Side-angle tracking shot showing her graceful walking style.

* Beautiful portrait close-up as she gently adjusts her hijab.

* Detailed macro shot of the blouse fabric, buttons, and stitching.

* Final wide shot of her walking away through the city.

Visual style: Ultra-realistic luxury fashion advertising, natural golden-hour sunlight, cinematic camera movements, shallow depth of field, realistic fabric physics, premium editorial photography, smooth transitions, 4K quality.

Format: Vertical 9:16, approximately 30 seconds.

Important: Maintain consistent facial identity, hijab, outfit, accessories, and body proportions throughout every scene.

How much should a robot policy trust each simulated demonstration when only a few real ones exist? BEACON, a NeurIPS 2026 paper from @hankyang94's group at Harvard with Brown, learns this instead of fixing a sim-to-real mixing ratio.

It trains a Diffusion Policy together with a weight for each simulated training sample. The weights come from a domain-adaptation bound (Best-Effort Adaptation): a sample that sits far from the real data gets less say in training.

On a Franka arm with 500 simulated and 40 real demonstrations, a sim-only policy scores 0 and a real-only one 0.08. BEACON reaches an average real-robot score of 0.79, against 0.62 for the best baseline, and 0.83 with two simulated sources.

The surprising part: closer feature alignment does not mean better transfer. When objects start outside the demonstrated region, stacking with the alignment baseline MMD falls from 0.40 to 0.05, while BEACON keeps 0.35.

A recent post on DiscoDemo (https://t.co/z0ltBGBiU4) covered generating extra demonstrations with RL; BEACON is about how much each such demonstration should count. Work led by Antong Zhang and Han Qi. Paper: https://t.co/ZmpHgjTcuq

Alice in Wonderland, but shot like a fashion campaign.

This clip was made with Vivix W1, and the first thing that got me is the texture.

The fur on the coats, the velvet on the Queen's cape, the tiny details on the giant mushrooms. It all holds up even when the characters start moving.

The motion feels natural too. The Hatter's little dance, Alice walking across the lawn with her mallet, the Rabbit's coat swinging with every step. And each character stays the same from shot to shot.

That's impressive visual quality for a model that's also built to keep generation fast and costs low.

Voice AI is now good enough that preference and human-likeness can be scored as separate targets.

@voicearena_ai launched a new benchmark, Turing TTS to score the second one directly: listeners hear the same sentence from a person and from a model, then pick the person.

How often they pick the model is the Fool Rate. 50% would mean listeners can’t tell.

Even the best model, Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS, fooled them about 10% of the time.

On Voice Arena’s preference board, the top four models are statistically tied. Measured against a human, the whole field still has a long way to go.
